messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 54

It is Tuesday in October, three years ago. Aris walks home from a community center meeting, carrying a reusable bag with groceries and a sketchbook their partner gifts them. A traffic stop three blocks from home draws a crowd. Aris slows to watch, hands visible, breath steady. Then a cruiser pulls up behind them, lights flashing. An officer steps out, commands sharp, voice low. Aris tries to speak, to explain they are not involved, but the cadence of the officer’s words—demanding compliance, stepping closer, hand resting on a belt—triggers something primal. They remember the weight of their own body suddenly feeling like a liability. When the officer’s grip closes around their upper arm, Aris goes still. They do not fight. They count the cracks in the pavement until the cruiser doors slam shut. The encounter lasts four minutes. The aftermath lasts longer. In the weeks that follow, Aris stops leaving the house after dusk. Work, where they lead a backend development team, becomes a landscape of quiet panic. They start timing their commute, taking backstreets, avoiding intersections with traffic cameras. On video calls, they mute themselves during stand-ups, staring at their own reflection in the darkened monitor. Code, once a space of logical flow, now feels like a trap. Debugging a race condition becomes unbearable when the screen flickers; every freeze echoes the moment their own body freezes. They sleep with their laptop open on the coffee table, half-watching pull requests like a substitute for vigilance. Their partner, Priya, notices the shift first. “You are here, but your eyes aren’t,” Priya says, touching Aris’s shoulder. Aris flinches, then nods, then apologizes, then promises it is just stress. The silence between them grows. At forty-six, Aris has spent years building systems that run predictably. Now they build walls instead. They and Priya rearrange their apartment—mattresses pushed against the living room wall, a doorstop under the bedroom door, a habit of leaving every porch light on. Aris stops attending their sister’s wedding in March because the thought of crowds, of unfamiliar faces, of someone raising a voice makes their palms sweat. They keep checking the lock on their front door. Three times. Every morning. When the news plays a familiar cadence of sirens in the background, their hands tremble. They breathe through it. They tell themselves they are safe. They do not always believe it. They take a symptom assessment online. The screen displays a number. Fifty-four. It feels less like a score and more like a full house. All the rooms locked. All the windows painted over. Now, Aris sits in the corner of the conference room, knees drawn to their chest, fingers tracing the seam of their jeans. The afternoon light cuts through the blinds in parallel lines, and they keep counting them. When I ask how the week has been, they look at the wall, not me. “Same,” they say, voice flat. They still write clean code. They still laugh at Priya’s terrible puns. They still make chai every Sunday morning. They come to this chair, week after week, because staying still feels like the only thing they know how to do now. Last night, when the car alarm goes off down the street, they are under the kitchen table before they even know they have moved. They count the cracks in the floor. They wait. They return next Thursday.
